summary.text: 干 is an old graph interpreted chiefly as a shield, with an early reported use for defense. In simplified Chinese it also writes the words traditionally written 乾 “dry” and 幹 “trunk”; these spelling correspondences do not show that either word developed from “shield”.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph as a whole is interpreted as depicting a shield, not as a compound of smaller sound and meaning parts. Some proposed Shang examples are disputed; the secure attestation identified here is a mid-Western Zhou bronze inscription.

components.text: The whole graph is interpreted chiefly as a shield, sometimes described with feather decoration. A competing interpretation identifies some oracle-bone forms with 單, depicting a forked hunting implement; this is a whole-graph analysis, not a division into smaller parts.

history.text: Some Shang forms have been proposed as 干, but their identification is disputed. A mid-Western Zhou bronze inscription is the secure attestation identified here. Later Western Zhou forms regularize the forked top as a short horizontal stroke, which continues in later scripts.

The Han-period Shuowen account analyzes 干 as 反入 plus 一 and gives it the sense “offend” or “violate.” This is a historical explanation of the graph and its meaning, distinct from the shield interpretation.

uncertainties.text: The shield interpretation has substantial scholarly support, but the identification of some proposed Shang signs and the distinction between 干 and 盾 in certain forms remain disputed. Another proposal treats some oracle-bone forms as variants of 單 depicting a forked hunting implement. The ancient name and pronunciation of the depicted object are not established here.

The correspondence of 干 to 乾 “dry” and 幹 “trunk” in simplified writing does not establish an ancient graphic derivation or semantic development from “shield.” The date and earlier spelling history of these correspondences are unresolved here.

senses.period: Securely attested by the mid-Western Zhou; proposed earlier Shang attribution is disputed.
senses.text: The graph is interpreted as a shield pictograph. Early defensive use and bronze examples meaning “shield” are reported; the earliest secure attestation identified here is mid-Western Zhou.

senses.period: Early inscriptional and textual use reported; exact first date unresolved.
senses.text: A defensive or protective use is reported in an oracle-bone example and a later bronze inscription. This fits the shield interpretation, though the sequence and date of this use are not established.

senses.period: Recorded in a Han-period dictionary; date of the word sense unresolved.
senses.text: The Han-period Shuowen account gives “offend” or “violate” as a sense and analyzes the graph as 反入 plus 一. It does not explain how or when this sense arose.

senses.gloss: dry (written 干 in simplified Chinese; traditionally 乾)
senses.period: Current simplified spelling; the word sense’s onset is undated here.
senses.text: In simplified Chinese, 干 writes the word traditionally written 乾. The dry sense is attested in the Book of Odes, but its first reading and any semantic development from “shield” are not established here.

senses.gloss: trunk; main stem (written 干 in simplified Chinese; traditionally 幹)
senses.period: Current simplified spelling; historical examples of 幹 do not date this spelling correspondence.
senses.text: In simplified Chinese, 干 writes the word traditionally written 幹. Cited early examples of 幹 mean a tree stem or the body's frame; they do not show that this word developed from the shield sense.

developments.text: A shield can be used for defense, making a connection between the object and defensive use plausible. The evidence does not establish a precise sequence of semantic change.

limitations.text: The dry and trunk words are written 干 in simplified Chinese and 乾 and 幹, respectively, in traditional writing. The spelling chronology and any semantic transition from the shield word are not established here.
The historical dictionary explanation records the “offend/violate” sense but does not establish its chronology or development.

overview.text: 干 is an old graph interpreted as a shield, with an early reported use for defense. In simplified Chinese it also writes the separate words traditionally spelled 乾 “dry” and 幹 “trunk.”

components.text: The whole graph is interpreted as a shield. Some proposed early forms are disputed, and the object's ancient name is not established here.

takeaway.text: The simplified spellings 干 for “dry” and “trunk” do not show that these words developed from “shield.”
